findings.issue: Source: "He sat himself down away from the ships with a face as dark as night". Candidate: "He moved like the night and sat down apart", which turns the dark face into a manner of movement.
findings.fix: So he prayed, and Apollo heard him. The god came down furious from the peaks of Olympus, with his bow and quiver on his shoulder. The arrows rattled on his back from the rage shaking him. He sat down apart from the ships with a face as dark as night. Then he shot an arrow among them, and his silver bow rang out with death. He hit the mules and the dogs first. Soon he aimed his shafts at the people themselves, and the pyres of the dead burned all day long.

findings.issue: Source "steeped in insolence and lust of gain" and "Sir Insolence!" became "wrapped in shamelessness and greed" and "Sir Shameless", changing the charge and duplicating "your shameless self"; also "take what I can get" became "whatever little I can get" (adds "little").
findings.fix: Achilles glared at him and answered, “You are steeped in insolence and greed. How can any Achaean obey you, whether on a raid or in open battle? I did not come here to fight because of any wrong the Trojans did me. I have no quarrel with them. They have never driven off my cattle or my horses, or cut down my crops on the rich soil of Phthia. A great distance lies between them and me, with mountains and the roaring sea. We followed you, Sir Insolence, to please you, not ourselves. We came to win satisfaction from the Trojans for your shameless self and for Menelaus. You forget all this. Now you threaten to rob me of the prize I worked for, which the sons of the Achaeans gave me. When the Achaeans sack some rich Trojan city, I never get a prize as good as yours, even though my hands do the greater part of the fighting. When the sharing comes, your share is by far the biggest. And I, naturally, go back to my ships with whatever I can get, and I must be grateful, once the labor of fighting is over. Now I am going back to Phthia. It is far better for me to sail home with my ships. I will not stay here dishonored, piling up gold and wealth for you.”

findings.issue: Candidate adds a position not in the source: "She stood behind the son of Peleus and seized him"; source only says she "seized the son of Peleus by his yellow hair".
findings.fix: The son of Peleus was furious. In his shaggy chest his heart was torn between two choices. He could draw his sword, push the others aside and kill the son of Atreus. Or he could hold himself back and check his anger. While he was in two minds, and was already drawing his mighty sword from its sheath, Athena came down from heaven. Hera had sent her, out of her love for both men. She seized the son of Peleus by his yellow hair. Only he could see her, and none of the others. Achilles turned in amazement, and from the fire flashing in her eyes he knew at once that she was Athena. “Why have you come,” he said, “daughter of aegis-bearing Zeus? To see the arrogance of Agamemnon, son of Atreus? Let me tell you—and it will certainly happen—he will pay for this insolence with his life.”

findings.issue: "rob his prizes from any man who contradicts you" became "go around the camp and rob" (adds "the camp"); "a feeble folk" became "a worthless folk" (changes the insult).
findings.fix: But the son of Peleus began abusing the son of Atreus again, for he was still in a rage. “Drunkard,” he cried, “with the face of a dog and the heart of a deer! You never dare to arm and go out to fight with the army, or to join our chosen men in an ambush. You shrink from that as you do from death itself. You would much rather go around and rob any man who speaks against you of his prize. You feed on your people, because you are king over a feeble folk. Otherwise, son of Atreus, this would be the last time you insulted anyone. So I tell you, and I swear it with a great oath. By this scepter of mine—which will never sprout leaf or shoot, nor bud again, from the day it left its stem in the mountains, since the axe stripped it of leaf and bark, and now the sons of the Achaeans carry it as judges and guardians of the laws of heaven—as surely as this, I swear that one day they will long for Achilles and not find him. On the day of your distress, when your men fall dying under the murderous hand of Hector, you will not know how to help them. You will tear your heart with rage that you insulted the bravest of the Achaeans.”

findings.issue: Source "you bore me doomed to live but for a little season"; candidate "you bore me to live only a short season" drops "doomed".
findings.fix: Patroclus did what his dear comrade had told him. He brought Briseis out of the tent and gave her to the heralds, who took her with them to the ships of the Achaeans—and the woman did not want to go. Then Achilles went off alone to the shore of the hoary sea. He wept and looked out over the boundless waste of waters. Raising his hands, he prayed to his immortal mother. “Mother,” he cried, “you bore me doomed to live only a short season. Surely Zeus, who thunders from Olympus, could have made that short life glorious. He has not. Agamemnon, son of Atreus, has dishonored me and taken my prize from me by force.”
